newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN impresses need for peace in Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: UN impresses need for peace in Afghanistan.

text.p: A one-day meeting of more than a dozen countries floundered in coming up with specific goals or programmes, but participants on Monday thought it remarkable that it took place at all.

"The important thing is that the players who have different interests sat down together without confrontation," said a key German diplomat. "They may do it again," he added, noting that one country or another had boycotted similar meetings when held outside of the United Nations.

The meeting also afforded Norbert Holl, the special U.N. represenative for Afghanistan, a chance to outline positions held by the warring factions and their conditions for taking part in negotiations, diplomats said.
Almost all countries at the meeting had at one time backed one Afghan faction or another and the conference called for the participants to use their influence toward peace in Afghanistan.

Most countries repeated Security Council and General Assembly resolutions that call for an end to fighting, a durable ceasefire, the demilitarization of Kabul and a political dialogue leading to a broad-based transitional government. Some said the protection of human rights was equally as important.

The fact that the meeting was held behind closed doors indicated Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali believed a freer dialogue would ensue. But judging from some of the printed speeches available, most nations restated their public positions.

Attending the meeting were envoys from the United States, China, France, Russia, Britain, Germany, India, Iran, Italy, Japan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Russia, Saudi Arabia, Tajikistan, Turkey, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

Pakistan's foreign secretary, Najmuddin Shaikh, reminded delegates of its long border with Afghanistan, saying, "No country, I repeat, no country has more to gain from peace in Afghanistan and no country has more to lose because of the continuation of unstable conditions."
While saying Pakistan wanted a broad-based government, Shaikh defended the Taleban, a purist fundamentalist group, that now holds more than half the country, including Kabul, the capital.

He said that its success was a reaction to anarchy and war weariness with people "ready to welcome any force that promised the disarming of the local brigands, the restoration of peace and the semblance of an honest administration, no matter how rough and ready its system of justice."

Referring to criticism that the Taleban has oppressed women and girls, Shaikh said Pakistan did not conduct such measures but they "should be viewed in the perspective of the traditions and customs of Afghanistan, and indeed of many other countries. But that is not, and cannot be the principal focus."
Iran, which supported the ousted government of Burhanuddin Rabbani, said the search for a solution in Afghanistan had become a hostage to extraneous and irrelevant considerations.
Javad Zarif, Iran's deputy foreign minister, in giving a list of principles that should be applied to countries' policies toward Afghanistan, included respect for human rights.
"Fundamental Islamic principles regarding the role and value of women are being trampled upon in the most brute form, regrettably in the name of Islam," he said.
In contrast to Pakistan's analysis, he said fierce fighting had forced more than 70,000 Afghans to flee their homes, a number of them crossing into neighbouring countries.

No Afghan faction was invited to the session, prompting the Taleban to denounce it. The movement wants to be recognised by the United Nations as the country's legitimate government but there is little chance this will happen in the next year.
